title: Structured Masked Diffusion for Shared-Codebook Unsourced Random Access Decoding
claim: A two-stage receiver turns superimposed user transmissions into evidence, and our decoder recovers the message set better and faster than alternatives.
layout: Single wide row, left-to-right; right-side stacked comparison panels beside the decoder
description: A wide left-to-right diagram of a two-stage receiver. At the far left, user icons (two active of several) each pick a codeword of colored symbol blocks, annotated K=2 active users. Their signals sum at a circled plus and pass through a gray 'Wireless Channel' cloud. This gives per-slot noisy colored observation columns y(1) to y(3). A blue box, 'Symbol-level soft detector (slot-wise AMP)', outputs an evidence matrix S drawn as a grayscale grid. A gray inset at top center shows the shared codebook: alphabet size Q=4, L=3 slots, M=5 messages. Top right, three colored panels (Classical Outer Decoders, Other Neural Networks, and the green CIDER panel) are marked with clock and target icons showing speed and accuracy as ticks or crosses. CIDER outputs the decoded matrix X-hat and the message set {3,4}. The eye goes first to the green CIDER block.
caption: Two-stage receiver pipeline. Active users transmit codewords from a shared codebook over a shared channel. A fixed AMP-based symbol detector converts slot observations into the evidence matrix S, and the multiuser decoder maps S to an unordered set of decoded codewords.
abstract: In shared-codebook unsourced random access (URA), a receiver must recover an unordered set of messages from simultaneous transmissions. Its outer decoder assembles ambiguous slot-wise evidence into distinct codewords while enforcing parity constraints. We propose CIDER, a learned outer decoder that combines masked-diffusion refinement with cross-row demixing and parity-aware propagation on the code's Tanner graph. At higher per-bin loads, quality-guided remasking selectively re-decodes low-confidence rows. On the evaluated GF(64) LDPC codes at $K=2$, CIDER has lower measured symbol and codeword error rates than SIC-BP and FFT-BP at all four code lengths. In same-GPU decoder-only measurements, the deployed mixed-precision implementation is $8.2\times$ to $167\times$ faster than our optimized FFT-BP implementation across those lengths. We also evaluate higher loads, estimated user counts, and detector mismatch. Code is available at https://github.com/jiyunyoung/CIDER/tree/neurips-2026.
